old_cards.name: The sequence, start to finish
old_cards.teaser: Camekân, göbek taşı, kese, foam, rinse — allow ninety minutes to two hours, and do not plan anything after it.
old_cards.body: An Ottoman bath is one room type repeated: a cold entrance hall, a warm transitional room, a hot room, and a furnace you never see. You arrive into the camekân (also written camegâh), the domed hall, and sign in at reception. You get a numbered key and a cabin, you strip, you wrap. Then you walk into the hararet — the hot room — and lie on the göbek taşı, the raised marble platform heated from beneath, until your skin softens. Kılıç Ali Paşa puts that wait at fifteen to twenty minutes and it is not filler; the scrub does not work on cold skin. Only then does the attendant come. Kılıç Ali Paşa puts the whole thing at ninety minutes to two hours; Süleymaniye runs a fixed 15 + 30 + 30 + 30 minute block. There is no sauna and no pool in any of them — Kılıç Ali Paşa says so flatly in its own FAQ, because Ottoman bath culture never had either. How it works — 1. Camekân — sign in, take your key, go up to the cabin. 2. Undress, put on the peştemal and slippers, valuables to reception. 3. Hararet — lie on the göbek taşı, 15–20 minutes, until you are sweating properly. 4. Kese — the attendant scrubs you with a coarse mitt, no soap. Note the houses differ, and one contradicts itself: Kılıç Ali Paşa's illustrated guide says 15–20 minutes while its own FAQ says 25–35; Süleymaniye allots 30 minutes to scrub, soap wash and soap massage together. At Kılıç Ali Paşa the kese is done sitting beside a kurna (marble basin) rather than on the platform, a stated hygiene rule; at Süleymaniye it is done on the marble next to the kurna. 5. Foam — lather worked out of a cloth bag and poured over you, with a gentle rub-down. 6. A second pass with a loofah, then hair and scalp washed. 7. Rinse from the kurna with a bowl. Step out to the soğukluk if the heat turns on you. 8. Fresh dry peştemal and towel, back to the camekân, sit, drink, cool down properly before the street. Etiquette — You are washed by someone; you do not wash yourself, unless you have specifically booked a self-guided session (Zeyrek's 'The DIY' is the one on this list). Voices stay low — Kılıç Ali Paşa and Galatasaray both ask this in writing. Photographs are restricted: Zeyrek permits them only in the cold room and not involving other guests, Kılıç Ali Paşa only where management designates, Süleymaniye only in the lobby. Food and drink are banned in the wet rooms outright at Zeyrek and Kılıç Ali Paşa. Come neither on a full stomach nor an empty one, and do not drink alcohol first — both are house advice, not folklore. The catch — The heat is real: Süleymaniye publishes 38–40°C at 65–72% humidity, and Hürrem Sultan states its göbek taşı at 42°C with the private rooms at 48°C. If you have never done this, the first fifteen minutes are the hard part and the kese is more abrasive than you expect. Pouring cool water over yourself from the kurna at any point is normal and nobody will mind — Süleymaniye explicitly invites it.

old_cards.name: What you wear, and the nudity rule
old_cards.teaser: You are not naked. In most of these houses being fully naked is explicitly forbidden.
old_cards.body: The peştemal — a flat-woven cotton wrap — is the whole costume, and it stays on. Kılıç Ali Paşa states it in writing: it is not permitted to be completely nude on the premises, and you must be covered from the waist down. Galatasaray prints the same rule in Turkish on its booking pages. This is the most common false expectation people arrive with, in both directions: some brace for a nudity ordeal that does not happen, others strip off and get corrected. Underwear or a bikini bottom stays on under the wrap. Zeyrek keeps disposable underwear on hand but still advises bringing your own spare; Süleymaniye goes furthest and hands women a bikini, shorts and a peştemal, and men shorts, while welcoming your own swimwear instead. How it works — Every house on this list provides peştemal, towel and slippers in the price, and most add soap or shampoo. You do not need to bring a towel. What you should bring is a spare pair of underwear, or swim shorts, or a bikini — whatever you wear in comes out wet and stays wet. Ağa notes women may bring their own bikini; Zeyrek and Kılıç Ali Paşa both advise spare underwear or a swim bottom. The tell — Bring one spare pair of dry underwear. It is the difference between walking out comfortable and walking out damp for the rest of the day. Etiquette — Wrap covers waist to knee, minimum. Leave watches and jewellery in the locker — Süleymaniye asks for this by name, and everything metal gets uncomfortably hot on the göbek taşı. Sunburn, open wounds or damaged skin: Galatasaray advises you not to enter at all, and Zeyrek will not serve you. The catch — Items provided are for use on the premises only. Kılıç Ali Paşa and Galatasaray both state that if you want a peştemal to keep, you buy one in their shop.

old_cards.name: The hamam, and the clock on the door
old_cards.teaser: Four rooms, ninety minutes, and the one thing that goes wrong more than any other: turning up in the wrong half of the day.
old_cards.body: Most historic Istanbul hamams give men and women the same marble at different hours, and the session times are the single most important thing to check before you cross the city. Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı, Sinan's bath of about 1583 for the crews of the Ottoman navy — already covered in this guide's bathhouse section — publishes the split on its own site and it is unambiguous: women 08:00–16:00, men 16:45–23:30. That is the shape of the problem in one line. A woman arriving at five in the afternoon does not get in; a man arriving at eleven in the morning does not either. Süleymaniye Hamamı in Sinan's complex above the Golden Horn is the outlier that solves it a different way: its own site describes a communal experience designed for couples and families, in a shared space, in swimwear it provides, with partners scrubbed and massaged together rather than separated — the one historic hamam where two people go in through the same door. Children under sixteen are not admitted there, which catches families out. How it works — Soyunmalık or camekân: a lockable cubicle, strip, peştemal wrapped at the waist, wooden clogs. Sıcaklık: lie flat on the göbektaşı, the heated marble slab in the middle, and do nothing for twenty to thirty minutes until you are properly sweating. Kese: the attendant works you over with a coarse mitt and the dead skin comes off in visible grey rolls — it is not gentle and it is the point. Köpük: a pillowcase whipped full of air and soap, emptied over you as foam, then a wash. Rinse by scooping from the kurna, the marble basin, with a tas — you never get into the basin. Then back out to the changing room, wrapped in dry towels, for tea, until you stop sweating. Ninety minutes end to end. The tell — Ask which package you have bought before you undress. In most houses 'hamam' on its own means the room and nothing else; kese and köpük are separate lines, and the gap between the door price and the real price is often double. Ask for the total, not the entry. Etiquette — Men keep the peştemal on the entire time, without exception. Women: practice in the women's session varies and nobody polices it — take bikini bottoms and a top, and follow the room rather than a guidebook. Do not climb into the kurna. Bring flip-flops, a comb and a second pair of underwear. Tip the tellak (men) or natır (women) in cash, into their hand, separately from what you paid at the desk. The money — Süleymaniye Hamamı publishes a flat €90 per person on its own site (read 16 Aug 2026) for a two-hour visit — 15 minutes welcome, 30 on the marble, 30 of peeling, soap wash and massage, 30 of refreshments — including a private lockable changing room, peştemal, towels, slippers and swimwear, and states there are no additional or hidden charges. No other hamam named here publishes a figure. Everywhere else, ask for the all-in total before you undress. The catch — Do not book a kese after a day in the sun. Nobody will talk you through the sequence unless you ask, and the staff at the big restored houses are working a queue. Two specific warnings from checking on 16 August 2026. Tarihi Galatasaray Hamamı in Beyoğlu is trading and its own site gives 09:00–21:00 — but it states nothing anywhere about gendered sessions or separate wings, and OpenStreetMap gives it 07:00–22:00 instead, so both the hours and the gender question have to be settled by telephone on (0212) 252 42 42 before you go. Süleymaniye's own site publishes no opening hours at all; the 10:00–21:00 you will find quoted comes from an OpenStreetMap record last checked in February 2023, which also tags it reservation-required and cash-only — verify all three when you book. And be clear-eyed about the room: the famous baths in the old city are now almost entirely visitors, as this guide's own hamam section says. For marble with locals in it, look at a working neighbourhood hamam and phone for the session times, because those are the detail most often wrong online. Anchor for the gendered clock — Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı, Kemankeş Mah., Hamam Sok. No:1, Tophane/Karaköy, Beyoğlu · Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı: women 08:00–16:00 · men 16:45–23:30 (own site, read 16 Aug 2026). Tarihi Galatasaray Hamamı: 09:00–21:00 per its own site, 07:00–22:00 per OpenStreetMap — sources disagree, and gendered sessions are not stated; phone (0212) 252 42 42. Süleymaniye Hamamı: no hours published on its own site. Zeyrek Çinili Hamam and Cağaloğlu, both in this guide's bathhouse section, carry their own clocks — check each.
