old_cards.name: Gendered hours — the way this trip actually fails
old_cards.teaser: Four systems across nine buildings, and two houses that do not publish the split at all. Get it wrong and you have crossed a city to a locked door.
old_cards.body: There is no single rule in Istanbul. Some baths are çifte — twin buildings under one roof, a men's half and a women's half behind separate street doors. Some are a single bath sliced by the clock, with a dead changeover in between. Some are mixed and take couples and families together. And at least one is currently not serving women at all. Two things bite hardest. First, the last reservation is often hours before closing, so the published closing time is not when you can still turn up. Second, two houses on this list — Cağaloğlu and Galatasaray — describe men's and women's sections but publish only a single undifferentiated hours line, so which section runs when is simply not on their websites. Phone them. Do not generalise from a guidebook, and do not trust a third-party listing over the house's own page. Etiquette — If you are a couple hoping to bathe together, only the mixed houses allow it. At every other address you are separated at the door and no amount of asking changes it. Süleymaniye goes the other way and refuses to separate couples once you are inside — and words its couples session as 'couples & families (Man & Woman)', which is worth knowing before you book. The catch — Hours also move with the season. Cağaloğlu runs 09:00–22:00 Monday to Thursday and 09:00–23:00 Friday to Sunday, but drops to 11:00–21:00 in its winter season — three hours shorter, with no published switchover date. Zeyrek is closed Mondays entirely. Galatasaray's online booking widget displays its time slots in the Africa/Juba timezone, which is a site misconfiguration rather than a joke — do not trust the times it shows you without confirming by phone. THE FOUR SYSTEMS, read from the houses' own pages 16 Aug 2026. (1) SEPARATE SECTIONS, BOTH RUNNING: Çemberlitaş — daily 06:00–00:00, house confirms separate men's and women's sections each with same-gender attendants. Zeyrek Çinili — Tue–Sun 08:00–22:00, closed Mondays, house confirms men and women served in separate areas. Üsküdar Çinili — men 07:00–22:00, women 08:00–19:30, two separate street doors and two separate phone lines. Ayasofya Hürrem Sultan — daily 08:00–22:00, mirrored men's and women's halves on one axis, listed as separate men's and women's services. (2) ONE BATH SPLIT BY THE CLOCK: Kılıç Ali Paşa — women 08:00–16:00, men from late afternoon to 23:30. WARNING: the house's own site gives two different men's start times, 16:30 on its contact page and 16:45 in its site footer. Treat the changeover as approximate and confirm by phone. CRITICAL: last reservation is 14:15 for women and 22:00 for men, so the closing times are not arrival times. (3) MIXED, COUPLES AND FAMILIES TOGETHER: Ağa Hamamı — daily 10:00–22:00, arrive by 20:00. Süleymaniye — couples and families daily 10:00–21:00. (4) NOT PUBLISHED, OR RESTRICTED: Cağaloğlu and Galatasaray publish hours but no gender split — phone before you set out. Süleymaniye's ladies-only session is closed until 5 September 2026 and its men-only session is 06:00–10:00 every day except Sunday, so a woman travelling alone cannot use that bath at present.

old_cards.name: The money, the extras and the hard sell
old_cards.teaser: The massage is not in the bath price. It has never been in the bath price. Say no or budget for it.
old_cards.body: Two houses state it in writing and the rest operate the same way: the traditional hammam ritual does not include an oil massage. Kılıç Ali Paşa — 'a traditional hammam ritual treatment does not include a massage. A separate reservation is required.' Galatasaray — the same line in Turkish, asking you to declare it when you book. A massage means a separate room, a separate therapist, a separate booking and a separate bill, and at Kılıç Ali Paşa it costs more than the bath itself (₺4,600 for fifty minutes against ₺4,300 for the ritual). Expect it to be offered warmly while you are wet, wrapped and in no position to negotiate. Decide before you go in. The second lever is currency and payment method. Kılıç Ali Paşa gives 5% off for cash and accepts sterling, euros, dollars and lira but not American Express. Ağa publishes card and cash prices side by side and the gap is ₺500 on a ₺3,600 package — about 14%. Çemberlitaş prints lira and euro figures on the same list, and those two numbers are not automatically the same money on the day. How it works — THE LADDER — house lists read 16 Aug 2026, cheapest way in first. Üsküdar Çinili — NOT PUBLISHED, cash only, phone the section you need. Galatasaray — NOT PUBLISHED, phone +90 212 252 42 42. Çemberlitaş entrance, no time limit — ₺2,900 / €57. Ağa entrance only — ₺1,800. Ağa traditional package — ₺3,100 cash / ₺3,600 card. Kılıç Ali Paşa traditional ritual — ₺4,300. Zeyrek 'The DIY', self-guided — €80; its shortest attended treatment €125. Süleymaniye, all-in, 1h45 — €90. Cağaloğlu — €95 to €400. Ayasofya Hürrem Sultan — €110 for 45 minutes to €300 for 110. Comparing lira and euro houses is arithmetic you must do yourself; Çemberlitaş's own dual pricing implies roughly ₺51 to the euro, which is a useful yardstick but is the house's internal rate, not a market rate. Etiquette — On tipping: only Süleymaniye publishes a policy, stating gratuities are entirely optional and at your discretion. Nobody else says anything, which in practice means the attendant will expect something. Decide your number and separate the notes before you undress, because otherwise you are doing that arithmetic wet, in a peştemal, in front of the person you are tipping. The catch — Watch the payment mechanics, not just the price. Süleymaniye takes a non-refundable deposit online and collects the balance IN CASH on arrival (EUR, USD or TRY) — so its '€90, no hidden charges' still means arriving with cash. Üsküdar Çinili states plainly that credit cards are not accepted at all. And prices in Turkey move fast with inflation while the euro-denominated houses re-sticker often: treat every figure here as a band and the date attached to it as the point of the exercise. Where a house prices in euros it is telling you plainly who its customers are.

old_cards.name: Who should not go in
old_cards.teaser: Two of these houses will refuse you at the door, and they are right to.
old_cards.body: This is a 40°C room at around 70% humidity with a stranger applying pressure to your body for half an hour, and the houses take the medical side more seriously than most spas. Zeyrek publishes the longest list: hammam services are not recommended for guests with cardiovascular disease, high or low blood pressure, respiratory disease including asthma, bronchitis and COPD, diabetes, urinary tract infection, recent surgery or cancer treatment — and guests with severe skin problems such as burns, allergies, open wounds, or with epilepsy, cannot be served at all. Zeyrek also does not recommend the hammam for pregnant women. Galatasaray goes further and states outright that it does not serve guests with heart conditions, guests who are pregnant, or guests who are menstruating, and advises against entry with sunburn or damaged skin. Süleymaniye asks you to inform staff in advance of pre-existing conditions such as high blood pressure or heart conditions, and does not recommend admission to anyone more than two months pregnant. Etiquette — Tell reception in advance if you have a condition — Süleymaniye asks for this specifically, and Galatasaray asks you to check with your doctor if you are on medication. Do not arrive drunk or hungover; do not arrive on a completely full or completely empty stomach. Both are house advice. The catch — Age rules differ sharply and catch people out. Süleymaniye does not admit anyone under sixteen at all, and sixteen-and-over only when accompanied by BOTH parents; it also caps groups at four people and offers no group discount. Galatasaray requires under-eighteens to be accompanied by an adult. Zeyrek admits 0–5 free, runs a dedicated 'Little Bubbles' treatment for 6–11 under a same-gender parent, and charges full adult rate from 12. Kılıç Ali Paşa prices children 4–12 at ₺2,700 and takes 0–3 free. Süleymaniye also states it is not suitable for disabled access.

h-kilic-ali.group: The imperial houses — the architecture you are paying for

old_cards.group: The imperial five — the architecture you are actually paying for
old_cards.name: Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı
old_cards.teaser: Sinan built it for the crews of the Ottoman navy. One dome, one bath, and the clock decides whether you are allowed in.
old_cards.body: Mimar Sinan built this inside admiral Kılıç Ali Pasha's mosque and school complex to serve the levends, the crews of the Ottoman fleet, when Tophane was the working harbour. The house's own two pages date it slightly differently — 1578 to 1580 on one, 1578 to 1583 on another — so take it as late 1570s to early 1580s. The patron is worth knowing: born Giovanni Dionigi Galeni in Calabria, captured and set to work as a galley slave, he converted, rose to command the Ottoman navy, and appears in Italian sources as Occhiali and in Cervantes as Uchali. The hot room is a single great volume under a dome fourteen metres wide and seventeen high, which the house describes as the second-largest hammam dome in Istanbul — not the largest, despite what you will read elsewhere. Seven years of restoration ended with reopening in 2012, and Europa Nostra gave it a heritage award in 2017. Critically, this is not a çifte hamam: there is no second wing. One bath, sessions alternating by clock. It also documents its own ritual better than anyone else in the city, step by illustrated step, which makes it the best first hammam for someone who has never done this. How it works — Reservation requested. You enter the camegâh, sign in, take a numbered key, go upstairs to a locker and change. Peştemal and slippers on, underwear or bikini bottom stays. Then fifteen to twenty minutes on the göbek taşı in the hararet before anything begins. The kese is done sitting beside a kurna rather than lying on the platform — a hygiene rule they enforce. Foam bath from a cloth bag, then a loofah pass, then hair washed, then rinse. Retreat to the soğukluk when the heat gets much. Fresh peştemal and towel, then the lounge. Total: an hour and a half to two hours. The tell — Ask for the traditional ritual and nothing else. Water and tea are included; the massage is not, and never has been. Etiquette — Not permitted to be fully nude — covered from the waist down at all times. Bring spare underwear or a swim bottom. Voices low. Photos only where management designates. No alcohol on the premises under any circumstance, and no food or drink brought in. Sterling, euros, dollars and lira all accepted; most credit cards except American Express. The money — House list read 16 Aug 2026, in Turkish lira: Traditional Hamam Ritual ₺4,300. Children 4–12 ₺2,700; infants 0–3 free. Massages, booked separately and in a separate room: full body 50 min ₺4,600; deep tissue 75 min ₺7,000; sports 50 min ₺5,000; partial body 25 min ₺3,400; foot 25 min ₺2,900. VAT included. 5% discount for cash. The catch — No sauna and no pool — they say so themselves, because Ottoman bath culture never had either. And read the clock twice, then read the last-reservation time, which is the part that actually catches people: as a woman you are turned away from 14:15 even though the door says 16:00. There is no back-up wing to put you in. Kemankeş Mah., Hamam Sok. No: 1, 34425 Tophane, Karaköy, Beyoğlu, İstanbul (as published by the house) · Women 08:00–16:00, LAST RESERVATION 14:15. Men from late afternoon to 23:30, LAST RESERVATION 22:00. Every day. One bath, no second wing, no overlap. WARNING: the house's own site gives two different men's start times — 16:30 on the contact page, 16:45 in the footer — so confirm on +90 212 393 80 10 rather than timing your arrival to the minute. (House pages, read 16 Aug 2026.)

h-zeyrek.group: The imperial houses — the architecture you are paying for

old_cards.group: The imperial five — the architecture you are actually paying for
old_cards.name: Zeyrek Çinili Hamam
old_cards.teaser: Sinan's bath for the grand admiral, back in service after a thirteen-year restoration — with a museum built into it.
old_cards.body: Barbaros Hayreddin Paşa, grand admiral of the Ottoman fleet, commissioned it; the house credits Mimar Sinan, building during the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent, over a Byzantine cistern. The house does not publish a precise construction year on its history page, so treat the commonly quoted 1530s dating as convention rather than something you can source from the owner. The İznik tiles that gave the bath its name were lost long ago and are dispersed among European collections — the specific museums and the often-quoted tallies of recovered fragments and reconstructed patterns are widely repeated but not stated on the house's own pages, so they are left out here rather than passed on. What is documented by the house: the site reopened in September 2023 after a thirteen-year restoration, under The Marmara Group. What separates it from every other bath here is that it is also a proper museum, with the Byzantine cistern beneath the women's cold room carrying plaster-incised graffiti of galleys whose makers and date are unknown. Men and women are served in separate areas. How it works — Book ahead by phone (+90 212 521 21 61), WhatsApp (+90 537 305 28 66) or email. Arrive fifteen minutes early — a delay of fifteen minutes or more cancels your slot automatically. Everything is provided: peştemal, slippers, towels, shampoo, and disposable underwear if you need it. Every treatment closes in the cold room with a rose-geranium facial towel, Turkish tea and something sweet and savoury. The tell — 'The DIY' at €80 — a self-guided session with a single-use kese and traditional hammam soap after a short demonstration. It is the cheapest way into this dome, and for anyone who dislikes being handled it is the whole answer. Etiquette — Photographs and video only in the cold room, and not involving other guests. No outside food or drink, and none served in the warm or hot rooms. Bring spare underwear or swimwear. Cancel or reschedule at least 24 hours ahead by phone or email. The money — House treatment list read 16 Aug 2026: The DIY, self-guided — €80. The Original, 50 min — €125. Refresh, 70 min — €160. Flow, 70 min — €180. De-Stress, 90 min — €200. Total Reset, 105 min — €250. Reborn, 125 min — €300. Little Bubbles, children 6–11 — €80; 0–5 free; 12 and over pay adult rate. Standalone: full body foam massage 30 min €95; hand and foot massage 30 min €90. Multi-treatment packages take 25% off at six, 30% at twelve. Museum admission is a separate ticket — confirm current museum pricing and any free-entry or guided-tour scheme directly, as those pages were unreachable on 16 Aug 2026. The catch — Among the dearest bathing in Istanbul, though not the single dearest — Cağaloğlu's top ritual is €400 against Zeyrek's €300. The restoration is superb and also complete: this is a very polished room, not a rough working bath. Practical note: the site serves an incomplete TLS certificate chain, so some browsers will throw a security warning — the business is trading normally and this is a server misconfiguration, not a sign of anything wrong. Zeyrek Mah., İtfaiye Cad. No: 44, Fatih, İstanbul (as published by the house) · Tuesday to Sunday 08:00–22:00. Closed Mondays. Last recommended booking 20:30. Allow about 90 minutes for washing and resting alone. Men and women in separate areas. (House practical-information page, read 16 Aug 2026.)

h-cagaloglu.group: The imperial houses — the architecture you are paying for

old_cards.group: The imperial five — the architecture you are actually paying for
old_cards.name: Cağaloğlu Hamamı
old_cards.teaser: The last great bath the empire built — and it was built to pay for a library.
old_cards.body: Constructed in 1741 under Mahmud I, begun by the architect Süleyman Ağa and completed by Abdullah Ağa, and endowed as a çifte public bath to generate revenue for the sultan's library inside Hagia Sophia. The bath paid for the books. Nothing on this scale followed it in Istanbul — the house calls it the last example of its kind built in the city. The two entrances are on different streets: the men's on the main road, up a staircase of ten steps between two marble columns with classic stalactite capitals, under an inscription of seven lines and twenty-eight verses; the women's on the side street called Hamam. The staircase exists because the street level rose over three centuries. The men's camekân is the showpiece — a high dome joined by segmented corner vault panels, a pool with a waterjet in the middle, and a lantern at the crown. The house claims, plausibly, to be the oldest Turkish firm still active today. How it works — Reserve ahead; phone +90 212 522 24 24 or WhatsApp +90 541 622 81 36. Men: find the columned door on Prof. Kazım İsmail Gürkan Caddesi and go up the ten steps. Women: go round to the side street called Hamam; it is a different door and people do get sent back and forth. The tell — Lokanta 1741, the restaurant in the same complex. If you are a chef with an afternoon, that is the reason to pick this one over the others — bath and lunch in the same 1741 building. Etiquette — Confirm which entrance before you set off. The two doors are on two streets and staff at one cannot check you in for the other. The money — House list read 16 Aug 2026, all in euros: The Istanbul Dream €95. Tip to Toe €135. Cagaloglu Hammam €170. The Ottoman Luxury Service €240. Sultan Mahmud The First €300. Elixir of Cağaloğlu Hammam €400. Bridal bath on request. Durations are not published alongside these figures, so ask what you are buying in minutes as well as euros. The catch — Euro-priced from €95 to €400 with nothing below it, and the room today is almost entirely visitors — come for the architecture and accept the rest. Winter hours are meaningfully shorter than summer, and the switchover date is not published anywhere. Alemdar Mah., Prof. Kazım İsmail Gürkan Cad. No: 34, 34110 Fatih, İstanbul (as published by the house) · Monday to Thursday 09:00–22:00. Friday, Saturday and Sunday 09:00–23:00. Winter season 11:00–21:00 — three hours shorter, with no published switchover date, so confirm by phone in the cold months. IMPORTANT: the house publishes a single hours line and does NOT publish which section runs when, despite describing separate men's and women's halves with separate street doors. Phone +90 212 522 24 24 and confirm your section and your door before you set out. (House pages, read 16 Aug 2026.)

h-suleymaniye.group: Plainer domes, stranger rules, and one that is still just a bath
h-suleymaniye.angle_note: the mixed bath: say 'mixed, for any party of men and women together' — never 'couples'

old_cards.group: Plainer domes, stranger rules, and the one that is still just a bath
old_cards.name: Süleymaniye Hamamı
old_cards.teaser: Wood-fired since 1550 — the one place couples bathe together, and the one where every attendant is male.
old_cards.body: A bath in the Süleymaniye quarter trading on 'Since 1550' and crediting Mimar Sinan, run quite unlike anything else on this list. Note the house's own arithmetic wobbles — its FAQ calls the building 472 years old, which would put it at 1554 rather than 1550 — so take the founding year as approximate. During its main hours it takes only couples and families, together, in a shared communal room, and it will not separate partners once you are in: they state flatly that couples must take the scrub and massage together and that requests to split are not accommodated. Their wording throughout is 'couples & families (Man & Woman)', which is worth knowing before you book. The furnace is the real thing: the house says the bath has always been heated only by natural oak wood fires, running twenty-four hours, holding the hot room at 38–40°C and 65–72% humidity. The published detail worth knowing before you book: all tellak are male, for every guest, women included. That is a deal-breaker for some people and it is far better to know now. How it works — Bookings are taken ONLY through their website — they state that reservations by phone or email are not accepted. Because of capacity they only open reservations for the next three days, so this cannot be locked in weeks ahead; plan around that rather than against it. The deposit is non-refundable, non-cancellable and non-transferable. Groups are capped at four people and there is no group discount. The session is a fixed one hour forty-five: 15 minutes arriving and changing, 30 minutes warming on the göbek taşı, 30 minutes of kese, soap wash and soap massage beside the kurna, then 30 minutes cooling down with refreshments and dressing. They ask you to vacate on time, and they mean it. The tell — The külhan. It is one of the few baths where you are told plainly that oak fires under the floor heat the marble under your back, burning continuously rather than fired up for a booking. Etiquette — A communal room shared with other guests, not a private suite. Nobody under sixteen is admitted; sixteen and over only when accompanied by both parents. Photos and video in the lobby only. Tell them in advance about any medical condition. Not suitable for disabled access, by their own statement. The money — €90 per person, house page read 16 Aug 2026. Includes a private lockable changing room, peştemal, towels, slippers, a bikini and shorts for women or shorts for men, hair dryers, and drinks in the cooling room. They state there are no additional or hidden charges and that gratuities are entirely optional. But note the mechanics: a deposit is taken online and the BALANCE IS COLLECTED IN CASH on arrival, in EUR, USD or TRY. The catch — Three things catch people. First: all attendants are male, always. Second: the ladies-only session is suspended until 5 September 2026, so right now a solo woman has no route in, and a solo man only has the 06:00–10:00 window, and not on Sunday. Third: the three-day booking window plus a non-refundable deposit plus a cash balance on arrival is a lot of friction for a day off — read it before you commit. They also do not recommend admission to anyone more than two months pregnant, and ask you to declare heart conditions and blood pressure. Süleymaniye Mah., Mimar Sinan Cad. No: 20, Fatih, İstanbul (as published by the house) · READ CAREFULLY, house page 16 Aug 2026. Couples and families: every day 10:00–21:00. Gentlemen only: every day except Sunday, 06:00–10:00. LADIES ONLY: CLOSED UNTIL 5 SEPTEMBER 2026. A woman travelling alone cannot currently use this bath at all. Confirm directly before you go — this is a dated notice and it will change. Heads up — A limited run or temporary regime — check before you plan around it.

h-aga.group: Plainer domes, stranger rules, and one that is still just a bath

old_cards.group: Plainer domes, stranger rules, and the one that is still just a bath
old_cards.name: Ağa Hamamı
old_cards.teaser: Mixed, priced in lira, itemised line by line — and well under the Sultanahmet houses for the same three things.
old_cards.body: A small bath in the Çukurcuma streets below Galatasaray, with the most transparent pricing in this section: entrance, scrub and foam listed as three separate numbers you add up yourself, with card and cash totals printed side by side. It is a mixed hammam — the house's own history page says it has served as a mixed bath for over a decade — which makes it, with Süleymaniye, one of only two places here where a couple can bathe together. Be clear about what that same sentence says, though: the house describes itself as serving only tourists. This is not a neighbourhood bath and does not claim to be. The building is a hot room with the göbek taşı plus two small hot halvet chambers off it with three kurnas each, the hottest part of the house and used only for washing, and a cold halvet to cool off in. The külhan is wood-fired, which the house makes a point of — most Istanbul hammams now run on natural gas. On the history: the house claims Mehmed the Conqueror built it in 1454 as the bath beneath a hunting lodge, that it was overhauled in 1844 under Abdülmecid, and that it is the first Turkish bath in Istanbul. That is the family's own account, not corroborated scholarship — read 'the oldest Turkish bath in Istanbul' as marketing and enjoy the bath on its own terms. How it works — Book through the site or phone +90 212 249 50 27. Kese, soap, shampoo, peştemal, towel and slippers are provided; women may bring a bikini. Because the pricing is itemised, you can genuinely take the entrance alone and do the rest yourself — that is ₺1,800 for the room, the cheapest published door on this list. The tell — Bring cash. It is the largest single discount published by any bath in this section, and at ₺3,100 the full traditional package undercuts every euro-priced house here by a wide margin. Etiquette — Mixed means mixed — swimwear norms apply and men and women share the hot room. If that is not what you want, this is the wrong address and Kılıç Ali Paşa or Çemberlitaş are the answer. The money — House list read 16 Aug 2026, itemised: entrance ₺1,800; kese (peeling) ₺900; foam bath ₺900. Traditional Package (all three) — ₺3,600 by card, ₺3,100 cash. Massage Package (adds a 20-minute oil massage, ₺2,000) — ₺5,600 card, ₺5,100 cash. Massage with face mask (adds ₺600) — ₺6,200 card, ₺5,700 cash. The cash discount is ₺500 on the basic package, about 14%. The catch — It is small, and between five and eight in the evening it is full. The 1454 founding story and the 'first Turkish bath in Istanbul' claim are the house's own and unverified. The house also states it serves only tourists, so do not come expecting a local room. And the mixed format is exactly what makes it either the best or the worst choice here depending on who you are travelling with — decide before you book, because there is no segregated alternative inside the building. NOT CONFIRMED from the house's own site — its 'Where are we?' page returns an error. In the Çukurcuma streets below Galatasaray, Beyoğlu. Phone +90 212 249 50 27 to confirm the door before you set out. · Every day 10:00–22:00, but arrive no later than 20:00. Busiest between 17:00 and 20:00. No closing day. Mixed throughout — not gender-segregated. (House FAQ, read 16 Aug 2026.)

h-uskudar.group: Plainer domes, stranger rules, and one that is still just a bath

old_cards.group: Plainer domes, stranger rules, and the one that is still just a bath
old_cards.name: Tarihi Üsküdar Çinili Hamamı
old_cards.teaser: 1640, two-metre walls, a tonne of firewood a winter, cash only — and nobody is going to explain anything to you in English.
old_cards.body: Cross to the Asian side for the one bath on this list that is not selling anything. It was built in 1640 for Kösem Sultan as one of four buildings in her Çinili complex — mosque, library, guardhouse and bath — and its original job was washing the masons putting up the Çinili Camii. The house adds a detail worth carrying: Kösem died once the women's section was finished, and her brother saw the construction through. Do not go for the tiles: the İznik work that gave the bath its name was stolen long ago, and the operators used blue stone on the walls instead to keep faith with the original idea. What survives is better than tiles. The walls are two metres thick. A single great kazan sits under the floor between the two domes, closer to the women's side, and roughly a tonne of firewood goes into it over a winter, the heat running through pipes in the floor and walls and the smoke out through flues called tüfeklik. The domes are pierced for light, and the three-hundred-and-seventy-year-old glass fanuslar set into them are physically lifted out when it gets too hot inside, to vent. The carvings on the marble and the kurnas are original. How it works — Phone the section you need — they are genuinely separate operations with their own numbers. Services offered are the plain three: kese, köpük masajı (foam massage), and an oil massage for women. They also run henna nights and bridal baths, which is what a neighbourhood bath is actually for. Nobody will walk you through the sequence, so read the ritual card above before you go. The tell — Go in winter, when the kazan is properly lit and the marble is hot all the way through. And look up: if the glass fanuslar in the domes have been lifted out, that is the ventilation system working, unchanged since 1640. Etiquette — You will very likely be the only foreigner in the room. Bring cash, bring spare underwear, keep quiet, follow what everyone else is doing, and do not photograph anyone. A few words of Turkish will do more for you here than anywhere else on this list. The money — NOT PUBLISHED — no figures anywhere on the house site, and nothing verifiable elsewhere. Ask on the phone when you call to confirm the hours. What IS published, and matters: CREDIT CARDS ARE NOT ACCEPTED. Bring lira in cash or you will not be bathing. The catch — STATUS UNVERIFIED — the strongest health warning on this page. The house website resolves and its pages load, but the content is stamped 2015, and hours, prices and current trading status cannot be confirmed from it. The house's claim that the walls came through 'the August earthquake' undamaged carries no year on the page and, given the site's age, most likely refers to the 1999 Marmara earthquake — it is repeated here as the house's claim, not as fact. Phone the specific section before you cross the Bosphorus — from Eminönü that is a ferry plus a walk uphill, and it is a long way to go for a locked door. Nobody speaks much English, nobody is selling you an add-on, and nobody is going to explain anything. That is the whole point and also the whole risk. Muratreis Mah., Çavuşdere Cad. No: 204, Üsküdar, İstanbul (as published by the house) · As published by the house — but the site's copyright line reads 2015, so treat these as a starting point and phone first. Men's section 07:00–22:00. Women's section 08:00–19:30. Open seven days a week including religious holidays, and open at night on arife (eve) days. Two separate street doors and two separate phone lines: men's +90 216 553 15 93, women's +90 216 334 97 10. Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-16 — call ahead.

r-tiras.angle_note: the trade, the tariff, and Rimedzo as the named walk-in

old_cards.name: Tıraş — the full berber
old_cards.teaser: Cut, cut-throat shave, ear-singe, cologne. A licensed trade, which means there is a printed tariff you are entitled to see.
old_cards.body: The berber is a licensed trade with its own chamber — the İstanbul Erkek Berberleri Usta ve Kalfaları Esnaf ve Sanatkârlar Odası, whose site was live on 16 August 2026 — and licensed shops display a tarife. That is the point worth carrying: unlike almost everything else in this section, you can ask to see a price list and it is a normal thing to ask. The ear-singeing that finishes the shave is not a stunt for tourists. A flame or a lit wick is run fast over the top of the ear and the cheekbone to take off the fine hair; it lasts two seconds and it does not hurt. The cologne that comes last is limon kolonyası, poured into your cupped hands — rubbing them together and putting them to your face is the entire response required. The whole thing is also, and mainly, a conversation you will not follow. How it works — Sit. Agree the service and the price before the cape goes on, and ask for the tarife if you cannot see one. Haircut first, then a hot towel over the face, then lather worked up with a brush, then the ustura — the open razor — with the grain and then against it. Ear-singe. Second hot towel. Alum block on the nicks. Cologne. A glass of çay while you look at the mirror and say nothing. Forty-five minutes to an hour for the full saç sakal. The tell — Ask for 'saç sakal' for the whole thing, 'sadece sakal' for the shave alone, 'ustura ile' if you want the open razor rather than the machine, and 'ense' for the nape. If you want the fine hair burnt off, you do not have to ask — it comes. Etiquette — Agree the price before, not after. Tip roughly ten percent in cash, more if a second person washed your hair. Do not haggle once the work is done. Most berber shops are men's rooms in practice — the chamber's own name is the men's barbers' chamber. Salons that take women advertise as 'kuaför'. The money — No verified city tariff figure is printed here. For a ceiling: a Beyoğlu shop that publishes its own list, 2.a Berber in Cihangir, asked 800 TL for a haircut and 1,200 TL for cut and shave on its own site as read on 16 Aug 2026 — that is a visitor-facing Cihangir rate, not the neighbourhood one. A residential shop works well below it. Ask, and ask for the printed list. The catch — I could not verify any 2026 chamber tariff figure on the chamber's own site on 16 August 2026, so this guide prints none — a wrong number here would be worse than no number. What is real is the spread. Shops around Sultanahmet, Taksim and the cruise quay quote in euros and land far above the neighbourhood rate, and the add-ons — wash, wax, face mask, shoulder massage — appear as separate lines on the bill without having been ordered. Ask what is included before, not after. Every neighbourhood in the city · Ordinary berber hours are roughly 09:00–20:00, six days; many close Sunday. Friday and Saturday are the busy days.

old_cards.name: Rimedzo Barber Shop
old_cards.teaser: One shop, one back street behind Hagia Sophia, and a price list you are told to look at before you sit.
old_cards.body: The shop's own site gives 1986 as its starting year — nearly four decades in the same doorway, three minutes from the busiest tourist square in Turkey, which is the improbable part. What makes it worth naming is not a technique, it is a habit: the site publishes its price list as an image and states plainly that prices may be updated at the shop, which is an unusual amount of candour in this postcode. Knowing the number before the cape goes on is worth more to a visitor here than any particular fade. How it works — Turn up. The site offers no online booking, so treat it as walk-in and expect to wait if the chair is taken — there is nowhere to sit but the street. Ask to see the list on the wall, agree the service, sit. A full cut and shave takes about an hour. The tell — The tell that you are in an honest shop rather than a tout's shop, anywhere in Sultanahmet: nobody stands in the doorway inviting you in, and the price is settled before the cape. Etiquette — Carry lira in cash. The site states no payment methods, so do not assume a card terminal. Tip in cash, separately. The money — Not published as a figure. The shop displays a list in-store and says prices may be updated there. Ask before you sit. The catch — Be honest about what I could and could not confirm. The site gives the address, the hours and the 1986 date; it gives no phone number, no staff name, no payment method and no price figures — the list exists only as an image the site tells you may be superseded in-store. Claims circulating elsewhere that it is cash-only or that the barber speaks English are not stated by the shop and are not repeated here. And Sultanahmet is still Sultanahmet: an honest shop in this postcode costs more than an honest shop in Fatih proper. Alemdar Mahallesi, Hoca Rüstem Sk. No:5/B, 34110 Fatih (Sultanahmet) · Monday–Saturday 09:30–20:30 · closed Sunday (the shop's own site, read 16 Aug 2026)

old_cards.name: 2.a Berber Barbershop
old_cards.teaser: One of the few shops in Istanbul that sells the cut-throat wet shave as a named service and prints what it costs.
old_cards.body: Most Istanbul shops will shave you with an open razor if you ask; this one sells it as the thing it does, describing itself in its own words as one of the few places in Istanbul to offer a professional hot-towel, cut-throat razor shaving service. It sits on a side street on the slope above Karaköy and publishes its prices in lira with euro and dollar equivalents beside them, which is honest about who walks in. The useful detail for anyone working a boat: by prior arrangement they will come to you, to a flat or to premises, and cut a whole crew in one go. How it works — Walk in, or call the mobile number on the site. Ask for cut and shave if you want the pair; the shave is listed separately. Hot towel, brush lather, open razor, towel again, cologne. Manicure and pedicure appear on the service list with no price against them — settle that one before it starts. The tell — The mobile service. Ask about it by phone before you assume a figure — the site quotes nothing for it and says costs are arranged case by case. Etiquette — Tip in cash on top of whatever you pay for the service. The money — The shop's own published list, read 16 Aug 2026 (site undated, © 2021): haircut 800 ₺, beard shaving 500 ₺, cut and shave 1,200 ₺, beard shaping 700 ₺, hair care 500 ₺; manicure–pedicure listed without a price. Confirm on the board inside. The catch — Read the price sheet as evidence, not as a quote. The site carries a © 2021 line and no revision date, and its own conversions imply roughly 57 lira to the euro — 800 ₺ shown as 14 €. Check today's rate against that: how far it has moved is exactly how stale the lira figures are likely to be. This is also a visitor-facing Beyoğlu rate. If you want the same razor at the ordinary price, walk twenty minutes into a residential street and point at your face. Altın Bilezik Sokak No: 2/A, 34433 Beyoğlu · mobile +90 532 397 70 73 · Monday–Saturday 09:00–20:00 · Sunday 12:00–18:00 (the shop's own site, read 16 Aug 2026)

r-sema.group: The turn — sema, and which one is prayer

old_cards.group: The turn — sema, and which one is prayer
old_cards.name: Sema — ceremony or show
old_cards.teaser: The tennure and the sikke are worn at all three tiers. Nothing about the costume tells you what you have bought.
old_cards.body: UNESCO proclaimed the Mevlevi Sema ceremony a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008. What is protected is the ayin — a fixed musical form in four sections, played by a vocalist, a ney player, a kudüm drummer and cymbals — and the turning itself: the left foot planted, the right foot driving the body around it, right palm turned up to receive and left palm turned down to give. The reason an honest question exists at all is legal history. The Republic closed every tekke in 1925, and what survived of the Mevlevi order survived by being reclassified as culture and put on a stage. The blur between rite and performance is not modern cynicism; it is the terms on which the thing was allowed to continue. So the useful test is not authenticity, it is the room: are you sitting in a theatre with a foyer, or on the floor of a hall where people are also praying? How it works — Three tiers, and they sort easily once you know they exist. One: a foundation's own ayin at its own centre — no ticket desk, two to three hours, mostly in Turkish, something to eat or drink offered, no applause at the end. Two: a ticketed programme held inside a real semahane, such as the museum lodge at Galata — genuine room, scheduled performance, small ticket. Three: a purpose-built show in a culture centre, sold through booking platforms. Hodjapasha in Sirkeci is the best known of these; I could not load its site on 16 August 2026, so confirm it is running and confirm its price before you buy. The tell — The clean tell for the bottom tier: anything advertised as a whirling-dervish evening with dinner and belly dancing. The sema and the belly dance have nothing whatever to do with each other, and putting them on one bill is the whole answer. Etiquette — No applause when a ceremony ends — the correct response is silence, and clapping marks you instantly. No flash. Do not leave while the dervishes are turning. Long sleeves and long trousers; women cover the head at a foundation's ayin; shoes off wherever the floor is a prayer floor. The money — Deliberately not stated. A foundation's ayin asks nothing at the door. A purpose-built show is priced like theatre. Anything charging show prices while presenting itself as a religious ceremony is charging you for the confusion. The catch — Even the top tier is not a spectacle put on for you. It is long, largely spoken, and the whirling may be forty minutes at the end of a three-hour evening. If what you want is an hour of turning with a seat, buy the show and do not feel bad about it; the dishonesty is only in selling the show as the sacrament. No ticket price is quoted in this section for any tier — the figures floating around resale platforms are unverifiable and the one price still printed on the official museum listing is years out of date. Check the seller's own page on the day. Beyoğlu, Fatih, Sirkeci

r-emav.group: The turn — sema, and which one is prayer

old_cards.group: The turn — sema, and which one is prayer
old_cards.name: Silivrikapı Mevlana Kültür Merkezi (EMAV)
old_cards.teaser: A foundation's own sema twice a week, with the discourse subtitled in English and no ticket desk — but you have to phone to find out where it is.
old_cards.body: Evrensel Mevlana Aşıkları Vakfı runs a fixed weekly programme at its own centre and publishes it in English on its own site, which carried a 2026 copyright when I read it on 16 August 2026. The thing that makes this useful to a non-Turkish speaker is specific and unusual: the discourse that opens each evening is a recorded video with English subtitles, so you can follow the evening rather than merely watch it. The centre is associated with Hasan Dede, who spent his life teaching there. There is an ikram — refreshments offered to everyone in the room — partway through, which is the marker that you are a guest at somebody's evening and not an audience. How it works — The published programme, read on 16 Aug 2026. Thursday: discourse video with English subtitles 19:30–21:00, zikir and prayer with hymns 21:00–21:20, refreshments 21:20–21:35, sema 21:40–22:30. Saturday: discourse video with English subtitles and refreshments 19:00–19:30, Sufi music concert 19:30–19:50, sema 19:50–20:30. Arrive for the start, not for the whirling — walking in at the end to catch the turning is what everyone notices. The tell — Being fed. Accepting the ikram, sitting on the floor and staying to the end are the three things that separate a guest from a spectator here, and none of them cost anything. Etiquette — Women cover the head; everyone in long sleeves and long trousers; shoes off; sit on the floor. No applause and no flash. You will be offered something to eat or drink and refusing outright is rude — take a little. The money — No admission figure published by the foundation. Take cash for a donation box and ask when you call. The catch — Three honest catches. First, the address: the foundation's own site publishes only its Şehremini office, not the hall, so telephone or WhatsApp before you cross the city — the street numbers circulating online for the Silivrikapı hall are inconsistent and this guide will not print one. Second, the clock: Thursday's sema does not begin until 21:40 and ends at 22:30, which puts you on Fatih tram platforms close to midnight. Saturday, finishing at 20:30, is the realistic one on a working day off. Third, no admission figure is published anywhere by the foundation — carry cash for a donation and do not assume it is free or assume it is ticketed. A foundation's calendar is not a box office and it moves for religious dates. The foundation publishes only its office address: Şehremini Mah., Küçük Saray Meydanı Cad., Adalan Pasajı No: 21-A/8, Fatih, İstanbul. Its site names the ceremony venue as the Silivrikapı Mevlana Cultural Center but gives no street address for it. Do not set out on a street number you found elsewhere — ring first. · Thursday 19:30–22:30 and Saturday 19:00–20:30, per the foundation's own published programme (read 16 Aug 2026). Confirm on +90 212 588 57 80, WhatsApp +90 552 524 34 94, or info@emav.org.

r-galata-mevlevi.group: The turn — sema, and which one is prayer

old_cards.group: The turn — sema, and which one is prayer
old_cards.name: Galata Mevlevihanesi
old_cards.teaser: A 1491 lodge with a genuine semahane. Visit it as a museum; treat the ceremony as a maybe.
old_cards.body: Founded in 1491 and known in Ottoman times as the Kulekapısı lodge, this is the best-known Mevlevi house in the city and the only place a visitor can stand inside a real semahane on an ordinary weekday. It closed with every other tekke in 1925, reopened as a museum in 1975 and was reorganised as the Mevlevi lodge museum in 2011. The hall is the reason to come: a wooden floor, mihrab and minber at the far end, the gallery where the musicians sat, and the side lodges now hung with marbling, calligraphy and hilye sheets. The courtyard tombs include that of the poet Şeyh Galib, who was sheikh here. It stands at the top of Galip Dede Caddesi, the instrument-makers' street, so the walk up from Karaköy earns the trip on its own. How it works — Buy the museum ticket and go in daylight — the room reads better empty than full. The ministry-affiliated museum listing gives the ceremony as Sunday at 18:00, one hour, 150 unnumbered seats, tickets online in advance. Seats are not numbered, so arriving early is the difference between the front row and the back wall. The tell — Go up to the gallery and look down into the semahane from where the musicians sat. That view is what the building was designed around. Etiquette — Shoes off on the semahane floor. If a ceremony is running, silence and no flash, and do not applaud at the end. The money — Museum admission listed at €7 on the ministry-affiliated museum listing. The 30 TL sema ticket on the same listing is stale and should not be budgeted on — verify before you count on it. The catch — The honest part, checked 16 August 2026. The museum listing states the museum is open, but its hours are contradicted by OpenStreetMap, which gives Tu–Su 09:00–16:30 against the listing's 09:00–18:30 — Turkish state museums also run separate winter and summer hours, so confirm on the day and remember it is closed Mondays and that the box office shuts an hour before the doors. The Sunday sema is run by an outside ensemble on an intermittent calendar rather than as a standing fixture, and the 30 TL ticket price on the museum listing is implausible against 2026 lira and reads as years stale — I could not reach a live ticket page for the venue to confirm anything. The museum is confirmed. The ceremony is not. Phone +90 212 245 41 41 before you build an evening around it. Şahkulu Mah., Galip Dede Cad. No:15, 34420 Beyoğlu · tel +90 212 245 41 41 · Museum: listing gives 09:00–18:30 with the box office closing 17:30; OpenStreetMap gives Tu–Su 09:00–16:30. Closed Mondays either way. Sema listed as Sunday 18:00, one hour — unconfirmed on any live ticket page.

r-cay.angle_note: the contract of the chair and the 1924 tea law; the gardens themselves are in the rooms to linger

old_cards.name: Çay bahçesi — the price of a chair
old_cards.teaser: One glass of tea buys the table for as long as you want it. That is the entire contract, and nobody will break it.
old_cards.body: A çay bahçesi is not a café. It is a public room with weather: chairs under a tree, a waiter with a tray, and no expectation that you will ever leave. Tea arrives in a tulip glass — ince belli, thin-waisted — on a saucer with two sugar cubes and a small spoon, poured from a stacked double pot: the demlik on top holds the concentrated brew, the kettle underneath holds the hot water, and the server mixes to your instruction. Açık is pale, koyu is dark, tavşan kanı — 'rabbit's blood' — is the deep red the second glass should be. Grandparents hold tables for four hours over a backgammon board. Students revise. Nobody is moved on. The economics only work because the glass is small and you will drink six. How it works — Sit down first, anywhere free — there is no counter and no queue. A waiter with a tray will find you within a minute. Raise a finger and say 'bir çay' for one, 'iki çay' for two. Order refills one at a time as you want them, not by the pot. Pay at the end, usually cash. In a municipal garden the same waiter serves two hundred people and will still remember your table. The tell — The tell for a real one: it sells tea and Turkish coffee and little else, plays no music, and lets you bring your own food — people arrive with bags of it. If there is a printed menu with sandwiches and a card machine, you are in a café with outdoor seating. Etiquette — Don't ask for milk. Don't tip beyond rounding up. Don't hold a table for four when you are one and the garden is full. If a stranger asks to share your table, they mean the table, not the conversation — say yes. The money — Deliberately not stated. A glass of çay is the cheapest line on any menu in Istanbul; the gap between a municipal garden and a waterfront one is several times over. Check on arrival. The catch — No price is given here, on purpose: tea prices have moved hard and any figure printed would be wrong by the time you sit down. What matters is the spread — a belediye çay bahçesi, municipal, plastic chairs, no view charge, costs a fraction of a waterfront garden pouring the same glass from the same double pot. Ask, or watch what the next table pays. Most tea gardens serve no alcohol, and many still take cash only. The four gardens this guide already names — Çınaraltı at Çengelköy, Pierre Loti above Eyüp, Moda Aile, and Çadır Köşkü in Yıldız — are the right rooms to do this in. Every shore and every park in the city · Mid-morning to late evening, weather permitting.

old_cards.name: Çay, and the tulip glass
old_cards.teaser: A law of 1924 put tea on the Black Sea coast, and it took over the whole day.
old_cards.body: Law 407 of 1924 put tea cultivation on a legal footing at Rize on the wet Black Sea coast; the aim Çaykur records is work and income for the Eastern Black Sea after the First World War. The first large harvest came in 1938, the first factory in 1947. It is served in the ince belli, the thin-waisted glass, held by the rim — and refusing one is close to rude. Ask for açık (weak) or koyu (strong); the stacked double pot lets the server mix it to order

old_cards.name: Nargile — the Tophane strip
old_cards.teaser: If the pipe arrives in under ten minutes it was not built for you. The whole point is the two hours.
old_cards.body: Nargile reached Ottoman Istanbul in the seventeenth century and was banned by Murad IV alongside coffee and tobacco on exactly the reasoning he applied to the coffeehouses: men who sit together talk. What is smoked now is mostly mu'assel — tobacco cut with molasses and fruit, sold by flavour. The older thing, tömbeki, is plain soaked leaf fired with raw coal, harsher and slower, still ordered by old men and still available if you ask for it by name. The ritual is entirely about pace: the pipe is packed, the coals are lit and carried over, and a boy works the floor with tongs and a fire tray, changing them twice across a session. Nobody hurries anybody. It is the cheapest way in this city to hold a table for a whole evening. How it works — Order the pipe before you order a drink. Say 'nargile' and a flavour, or say 'elma' — apple — and stop thinking about it. The maşacı brings coals and returns to change them; catch his eye, or ask 'köz alabilir miyim?' for fresh ones. A fresh disposable mouthpiece, an ağızlık, is standard — if one does not appear, ask. Never light a cigarette from the nargile coal; it is the one gesture that will get you a look from every table in the room. The tell — A real nargile house has a coal boy on the floor with tongs and a brazier, not a waiter with a lighter. Ask for tömbeki if you want to taste what this was before the flavours arrived. Etiquette — Pass the hose by the stem, never mouthpiece-first. One pipe per table is normal and sharing is normal. Nearly all nargile houses serve no alcohol — do not walk in expecting a beer. The money — Not stated — priced shop by shop and by who you look like. Ask the price of the pipe before it is packed, and expect the tourist-facing courtyards in the old city to be several times the Tophane rate. The catch — This is tobacco, smoked continuously for an hour or two. It is not the mild option because it passes through water, and no comparison figure is quoted here because none could be verified today — treat the numbers you see repeated online with suspicion and treat the activity as what it is. On the geography, be careful too. The Çorlulu Ali Paşa medrese courtyard, which this guide already names, is the famous one and is now heavily visitor-priced. The Tophane strip below İstiklal is where the same ritual runs at neighbourhood rates — but shop names there turn over fast and I could not verify a single individual business as trading on 16 August 2026. Treat it as a district, not an address. Walk it, and sit down in the room that has the coal boy. Tophane, Beyoğlu — below İstiklal, between the Kılıç Ali Paşa mosque and Istanbul Modern · Nargile houses run late, commonly to midnight or beyond. Best after dark, when the trade turns from passing to sitting. No individual opening hours verified. Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-16 — call ahead.

old_cards.name: Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medresesi
old_cards.teaser: A theology college courtyard where the students were replaced by nargile smoke.
old_cards.body: Çorlulu Ali Paşa built this medrese in 1708 on the old Divanyolu, the imperial processional road, as a working college. Its two courtyards now hold carpet dealers and one of the city's long-standing nargile and tea gardens — low stools, cushions, glasses arriving without being asked. It is the single good reason to sit down in the old city, which this guide otherwise tells you to eat your way out of. Yeniçeriler Cd. (old Divanyolu), Beyazıt, Fatih — between the Grand Bazaar and Çemberlitaş · tea and nargile, no alcohol

r-kahve.angle_note: the cup, UNESCO 2013, 1554, and the fal reading at Katina

old_cards.name: Türk kahvesi — Fazıl Bey, and the cup turned over
old_cards.teaser: One small cup, twenty minutes, and a foam you can judge the whole thing on.
old_cards.body: Turkish coffee is judged on the köpük, the fine head of foam, and the foam is a function of heat control: the cezve is brought up slowly and lifted off as it rises, two or three times, and never allowed to boil over. Get that wrong and you are drinking boiled coffee. Fazıl Bey's is the everyday Kadıköy counter that does it properly at an everyday price — a market-side room rather than a set piece, open eight in the morning until midnight, seven days, which makes it one of the few places in this section a chef finishing a shift can actually reach. Sand-brewing — kumda kahve, the cezve set into a tray of hot sand so nothing scorches on the base — is the version you will see photographed; be aware it has become largely a visitor-facing presentation in this city, and this guide could not verify any particular old bazaar house as still doing it. How it works — Order by sugar, which goes in before the boil and can never be added after: sade for none, az şekerli for a little, orta for medium, çok şekerli for sweet. Water arrives alongside and is drunk first, to clear the mouth. Do not stir. Drink to the last centimetre and stop — the rest is grounds. Then, if you want, invert the cup onto the saucer and let it cool. The tell — Judge the cup on the foam, not the strength. A proper one arrives with an even, fine head across the whole surface; a boiled one arrives flat, with a ring of scum at the edge. Etiquette — It is one small cup and it is meant to take twenty minutes. Do not order a second immediately. Turkish coffee closes a meal here, it does not open one. The money — Not published by either house. Fazıl Bey is an ordinary neighbourhood counter and is the benchmark for what a cup should cost; anything inside the Grand Bazaar will be a multiple of it. Ask before you order. The catch — On the Grand Bazaar alternative: Şark Kahvesi is a genuine old bazaar coffeehouse and is mapped inside the bazaar on Zenneciler Sokağı, not on the main artery as is often written. This guide could not verify its founding date, its brewing method or its current prices on 16 August 2026, and the recurring complaint about it in both Turkish and English is bazaar pricing — go for the vaulted room if you want the room, and do not expect value. Note also that the Grand Bazaar is shut on Sundays and public holidays, which catches people out, and that its hours are roughly 09:00–19:00 Monday to Saturday — confirm on the day. Fazıl Bey'in Türk Kahvesi, Serasker Cad., Caferağa, Kadıköy · tel 0216 346 16 15 · Fazıl Bey'in Türk Kahvesi: 08:00–24:00, seven days (the company's own site, read 16 Aug 2026; OpenStreetMap agrees, Mo–Su 08:00–24:00). Grand Bazaar: roughly 09:00–19:00 Monday–Saturday, closed Sundays and public holidays.

old_cards.name: Türk kahvesi
old_cards.teaser: Two Syrians opened the first coffeehouse here in 1554; the city never recovered.
old_cards.body: Hakem of Aleppo and Şems of Damascus opened Istanbul's first kahvehane in Tahtakale in 1554. Around fifty were counted in the city by the end of Süleyman's reign; Murad IV later banned the drink outright, on the correct assumption that men who sit together talk. UNESCO inscribed Turkish coffee culture in 2013 for the ritual rather than the bean: water first, a sweet alongside, the grounds left in the cup for the fal. ORDER sade, az şekerli, orta or çok şekerli — the sugar goes in before the boil, never after

old_cards.name: Katina Fal Cafe
old_cards.teaser: You drink the coffee, turn the cup upside down on the saucer, wait for it to cool, and hand your afternoon to a stranger.
old_cards.body: Kahve falı reads what is left after a Turkish coffee. Because the grounds are unfiltered and heavy there is always a residue, and the ritual is to invert the cup onto its saucer — some put a coin or a ring on the base — let it cool, then read the runs of grounds: down the inside walls for what has been, around the rim for what is close, on the saucer for the house. Between friends this happens everywhere in Turkey and costs nothing. Commercially it happens in a specific institution, the fal cafe, and Kadıköy is the city's fal quarter, with several within a few streets of Serasker Caddesi. Katina's own site says it has traded there since 2013, seven days a week, with a terrace over the neighbourhood, and lists kahve falı, tarot, katina, ebced, kum falı and su ve peri falı — and, in its own words, medyums. Its first instruction to a visitor is to book a place in the queue rather than turn up. How it works — Phone ahead — the site's own opening line asks you to. You order something to drink or eat; the reading is charged on top or absorbed into a table minimum. The falcı takes your inverted cup, turns it over, and talks for ten to twenty minutes. The convention is that you say as little as possible — volunteering information is considered to have spoiled it. The tell — The coin on the base of the inverted cup, and the wait while it cools. If someone reads the cup immediately, they are performing rather than reading. Etiquette — Book. Pay cash. Don't argue with the reading and don't push for specifics — the form is allusive on purpose. The money — No price published. Kadıköy fal cafes generally work on a table minimum plus a per-reading fee. Agree the figure before the cup is turned, and refuse an open-ended one. The catch — Three catches, and the first is that I could not confirm this business is still trading. Its website resolves but its security certificate has expired and the footer still reads 2013; the address, phone and hours below come from that unmaintained page and nothing else. Ring before you cross the water. Second, expect Turkish — none of the Kadıköy fal cafes advertise an English-speaking reader, and a reading through a translator is not a reading. Third, and seriously: this cafe advertises medyums alongside its falcıs, and the medyum trade in Turkey sits next door to a real fraud industry that works on people in trouble. A cup read over a coffee is harmless entertainment. Anything that escalates into paid follow-up sessions, lifting a curse, or a bank transfer is a fraud, and the correct response is to stand up and leave. Caferağa Mah., Serasker Cad., Pavlonya Sk. No:23/3, 34710 Kadıköy · +90 533 777 72 32 (per the cafe's own site, which appears not to have been maintained for years) · Listed as seven days, 11:30–21:00, on the cafe's own site — a page last dated 2013 and serving an expired certificate. Treat as indicative only and telephone first. Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-16 — call ahead.

r-serpme.angle_note: the ritual; the three breakfast houses are table cards: name them, do not retell

old_cards.name: Serpme kahvaltı — the Sunday
old_cards.teaser: Twenty plates, three hours, and nothing else planned for the day. It is an appointment, not a breakfast.
old_cards.body: This guide already explains what serpme kahvaltı is and where the word came from. What it does not tell you is that it functions as a scheduled event rather than a meal you drop into. The Istanbul version runs on Sunday from roughly ten in the morning to two in the afternoon; tables are held, not turned; and a serious kahvaltı house will not seat two people at a table for four at half past eleven without a booking. The structure matters practically: you make one decision, per person, and then the plates arrive together and keep arriving. There is no second round of ordering, no courses and no order of service. The commonest visitor mistake is treating it as a menu. How it works — Book, or be at the door when it opens. Order 'serpme kahvaltı, iki kişilik' — the count is people, not portions. The only thing you actually choose is the egg: menemen soft-scrambled with tomato and green pepper, sahanda yumurta fried in the pan, sucuklu yumurta with the cured sausage, or a plain omlet. Tea is poured and refilled without being asked and is normally included, but ask rather than assume. Turkish coffee comes at the end, which is the joke buried in the word kahvaltı — kahve altı, 'under coffee', the thing eaten before the cup. Two to three hours. Plan nothing after it. The tell — The markers of a serious table are bal kaymak — clotted buffalo cream under comb honey — eggs cooked to order rather than held in a chafing dish, and çay refilled before you notice the glass is empty. Add a bread basket replaced hot, and at least one plate you cannot identify. Etiquette — Do not ask for plates to be cleared as you go; the sprawl is the format. Do not ask for coffee at the start. Do not order à la carte alongside a serpme spread — it costs more and reads as a rejection of the thing you just sat down to. The money — Priced and displayed per person. No figure is given here — the spread between a neighbourhood house and a waterfront one, and between a weekday and a Sunday, is too wide for any single number to be honest. Read the board. The catch — The catch is arithmetic. Serpme is priced per head and quoted per head, so a table for two on a Sunday can cost more than dinner for two — read the board carefully, because the number on it is what one of you pays. The same house serving a weekday breakfast will put most of the same plates down for a fraction of it. The Bosphorus-front kahvaltı strips at Bebek, Çengelköy and Beşiktaş are where the price has run furthest ahead of the food and where the queue is longest. And for anyone working a boat with one day off: this eats the whole morning and most of the afternoon. It is the most time-expensive thing in this section by a distance, and it is worth doing exactly once. Beşiktaş, Bebek, Çengelköy, Moda — and every quarter's own version · Sunday roughly 10:00–14:00 is the institution. Kahvaltı houses generally serve from about 08:00 or 09:00; the better ones run breakfast into mid-afternoon, which is how to avoid the eleven o'clock crush — go at nine or go at three.

r-raki-balik.angle_note: choosing the fish by the kilo; the pacing of the sofra is in the bars fold

old_cards.name: Rakı-balık — choosing the fish off the ice
old_cards.teaser: The fish is not on the menu. It is on ice by the door, priced by the kilo you have not yet asked about.
old_cards.body: The rakı table's spine is cold mezes, then hot mezes, then one fish — and the fish is chosen rather than ordered. In a balıkçı or a meyhane with a counter you walk to the ice at the entrance, point at what you want, and it is weighed in front of you before it goes on the grill. That single step is where visitors lose money in this city more reliably than anywhere else, because the fish is priced by the kilo, the per-kilo price is frequently not posted, and a lüfer that looked like one person's dinner arrives at nine hundred grams. Ask 'kilosu kaç?' before you point, and ask to see the scale. A house that will not show you the kilo price has already told you what kind of house it is. How it works — Rakı and cold water arrive together; the spirit is drunk diluted and turns milky as the water goes in, and the water glass stays beside it and is drunk alongside. If ice is used it goes in last, on top of the mix — never pour rakı straight onto a glass of ice. Then cold mezes, unhurried, for the best part of an hour. Then hot mezes. Then the fish, grilled whole with nothing on it. Season decides everything: palamut from September, lüfer peaking in October, hamsi through December. Anything glossy and cheap in July is farmed or flown. At a market counter rather than a restaurant, ask 'temizler misiniz?' to have it cleaned. The tell — The tell of a real table is the pace: four hours, nobody's plate cleared early, and the drinking set by the food. Ordering rakı and then eating fast is the visitor's giveaway more than anything you say. Etiquette — You never drink rakı without food. The water glass stays full and is drunk alongside, not after. When glasses touch, the rim of yours goes lower than the elder's — a small gesture, and it is noticed. The money — Priced by the kilo and it moves weekly with the catch and the season. There is no fair number to quote and anyone quoting one is guessing. Ask the kilo price and watch the scale — that is the entire defence. The catch — The per-kilo trick is real, common and entirely legal. Kumkapı has the worst reputation for it. The Beyoğlu Balık Pazarı row off Sahne Sokak has thinned into meyhane tables and stalls, so it is now more restaurant than market. The counters that still work as markets — Kadıköy off Güneşlibahçe Sokak, Beşiktaş Çarşı, Üsküdar Balıkçılar Çarşısı — are where the price is honest, and are also where nobody will pour you a rakı. On buying your own fish and having it cooked nearby: some grills next to the fishmongers will do it and some will not, it is not a standard citywide service, and it is worth asking rather than assuming in either direction — do not plan an evening around it. Kadıköy's fish row off Güneşlibahçe Sokak · Beşiktaş Çarşı · Üsküdar Balıkçılar Çarşısı · Fish counters are a morning business and most are finished by early afternoon. The rakı table is an evening one and starts late — Thursday is the night, per this guide's own week.

old_cards.name: Çınaraltı, Çengelköy
old_cards.teaser: Chairs set under a plane tree said to be nearly a thousand years old.
old_cards.body: The name means 'under the plane tree', and the tree is the entire proposition: a vast çınar on the Asian shore at Çengelköy, its canopy over tables facing the water. The garden pours tea and coffee and nothing else — you are expected to bring your own food, and people do, in bags. No music, no backgammon, no nargile, open at any hour. It is the least commercial room in this guide. Çengelköy waterfront, Üsküdar — Asian shore · tea and coffee only, bring your own food

old_cards.name: Pierre Loti Kahvesi
old_cards.teaser: A hilltop coffeehouse from the 1800s, above the graves, looking down the Golden Horn.
old_cards.body: Evliya Çelebi knew this hill as the İdris Köşkü picnic ground. By the nineteenth century a coffeehouse called Rabia Kadın stood on it, and the French naval officer Julien Viaud — writing as Pierre Loti — arrived in 1876 and is said to have finished Aziyadé at one of its tables. The hill took his name. Ride the cable car up from Eyüp pier, then walk back down through the Ottoman cemetery: that descent is the reason to come. İdris Köşkü Cad., Eyüpsultan · teleferik from Eyüp pier, about three minutes · busiest at sunset

old_cards.name: Pierre Loti Hill
old_cards.teaser: Tea above a cemetery, the whole Golden Horn laid out below.
old_cards.body: Louis Marie-Julien Viaud, a French naval officer who published as Pierre Loti, turned his Istanbul sojourn into the 1879 novel Aziyadé and spent his free hours on this hill; the house is now a museum under his name. A cable car climbs from the Golden Horn shore to the terrace, which sits above Eyüp cemetery — long a favoured burial ground for its closeness to the tomb of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, over which Mehmed II raised a marble tomb and a mosque after 1453. Tea and nargile, and nothing whatsoever to plug in. Eyüpsultan · cable car from the Golden Horn shore · tea and nargile

old_cards.name: Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi
old_cards.teaser: The whole of Kadıköy, three generations of it, facing the Marmara over a backgammon board.
old_cards.body: A municipal tea garden on the slope above Moda's shore: umbrellas and plastic chairs under tall trees, the Sea of Marmara filling the view with the Princes' Islands on the horizon. Nobody is performing. Grandparents, students and dog-walkers hold tables for hours over tea and tavla, the food runs to sandwiches and toast, and half the room brought its own. This is what the Asian side does with an afternoon. Caferağa, Park İçi Yolu, Moda, Kadıköy · outdoor only, so weather decides · late afternoon into sunset

old_cards.name: İnci Pastanesi
old_cards.teaser: One dessert, one recipe, since the 1940s — then redevelopment moved the whole shop.
old_cards.body: İnci opened in the Cercle d'Orient building on İstiklal in the mid-1940s and built the business on one thing: choux balls filled with pastry cream under a chocolate sauce, the profiterol. It is the version every other one in the country is measured against. The shop was evicted in the early 2010s when the building was redeveloped; it went dark for about seventy days and reopened round the corner on Mis Sokak. Mis Sok. 18/A, Beyoğlu · roughly 08:00 to midnight, daily · order the profiterol and nothing else

old_cards.name: Markiz (ex-Lebon)
old_cards.teaser: Four Art Nouveau seasons were ordered from France; two are still on the wall.
old_cards.body: Lebon's patisserie was trading on the Grand Rue from the 1880s and became the salon of Pera, with Pierre Loti and Yahya Kemal among the regulars. Its Art Nouveau faience panels were ordered from France: four seasons commissioned, and only Spring and Autumn survive in the room. When Lebon moved across the street in 1940, Avedis Ohanyan Çakır opened Markiz in the room it left, keeping the tiles. It closed in 1980 and came back, panels and all, in 2003. İstiklal Cad. 360–362, Beyoğlu, at the corner of the Oriental passage · grand-café prices, not budget coffee

old_cards.group: Counters with the hours for it
old_cards.name: Kronotrop, Cihangir
old_cards.teaser: Sixteen hours a day of table, on the slope above Tophane.
old_cards.body: Kronotrop opened in 2012 as one of the first specialty roasteries in Turkey — its founder, Çağatay Gülabioğlu, was the country's first Q grader — and the Cihangir room is the flagship, on the slope above Tophane where a good share of the city's writers, editors and film people live. It runs 07:00 to 23:30, seven days a week. It is small and it fills, so the etiquette is one long session rather than a whole day at the same table. The chain has since passed forty branches across Turkey and beyond, with very different hours at each, so aim for this room rather than the nearest sign. Cihangir, Beyoğlu · daily 07:00–23:30

old_cards.name: Montag Coffee Roasters
old_cards.teaser: Own-roasted beans across three rooms, and the Kadıköy one is where you sit down.
old_cards.body: Montag roasts its own and runs rooms in Kadıköy, Moda and Bomonti. The Kadıköy shop is the one to sit in: counter downstairs, a quiet second floor, V60 and cold brew alongside espresso, and the kind of turnover that means the bag you buy was roasted recently. Beans by the bag if you are travelling on. Caferağa, Muvakkıthane Cd. 16/A, Kadıköy · 10:00–22:00, to 23:00 Fri–Sat · Baylan is at number 9 on the same street

old_cards.group: Counters with the hours for it
old_cards.name: Petra Roasting Co., Bebek
old_cards.teaser: Where the shore walk ends and the morning's work starts.
old_cards.body: The walk north from Arnavutköy along the water, past the wooden yalı , ends in Bebek — and this branch opens at half past seven on weekdays, which makes it the obvious place to put a morning after the best hour on the European shore. It is closed on Mondays, so build the walk around a Tuesday. Four further branches sit at Gayrettepe, Şişhane, Topağacı and Maslak if you are on the wrong side of the hill; the Şişhane one also closes Mondays, the rest do not. Bebek, Beşiktaş · Tue–Fri 07:30–20:00 · Sat–Sun 10:00–20:00 · closed Mondays

old_cards.name: Atatürk Kitaplığı
old_cards.teaser: A free reading room in Beyoğlu, open until nine, seven days a week.
old_cards.body: Sedad Hakkı Eldem — the architect who spent a career folding the Ottoman timber house into modernism — drew this as a culture complex of library, museum and exhibition halls; only the library was ever built. Koç Holding put the building up in 1973 and the collection moved in on 3 March 1981: around 228,000 books, 20,000 periodicals and 10,000 bound volumes of newspapers, alongside manuscripts, maps, albums and postcards. The city runs it, entry is free, and the hours do not move for the weekend — 09:00 to 21:00, every day. Gümüşsuyu, Miralay Şefikbey Sok. No:6, Beyoğlu · every day 09:00–21:00 · free

g-salt.angle_note: one home for SALT: the bank, the free building, the library and the open archive

old_cards.name: SALT Research, SALT Galata
old_cards.teaser: A bank built for the Galata money, emptied of it, handed to readers.
old_cards.body: Alexandre Vallaury built this as the headquarters of the Imperial Ottoman Bank, finished in 1892, and the bank worked from it until 1999. Han Tümertekin's conversion reopened the building in November 2011 as SALT Galata, holding the research library and the old Ottoman Bank Museum. Reading costs nothing, but SALT Research is a registered collection rather than a walk-in one: you sign up once and are issued a personal access pass, study areas are bookable in blocks of up to three hours, and nothing circulates. Outside, the stairs cut around 1870–1880 by Abraham Salomon Camondo, of the Ottoman-Venetian Jewish banking family whose street this was, still climb the hill. Maksut Aşkar's one-star Neolokal is upstairs in the same building. Bankalar Caddesi 11, Karaköy 34421 · SALT Research Tue–Sat 11:00–19:00 · free, registration required · closed Mondays

old_cards.name: SALT Galata
old_cards.teaser: The Imperial Ottoman Bank's head office, and it costs nothing to walk in.
old_cards.body: Alexandre Vallaury finished the Imperial Ottoman Bank's headquarters on Bankalar Caddesi in 1892, and the bank held the building until 1999. SALT took it in November 2011 and made it free: galleries, an open research library, a café and bookshop at street level, and the Ottoman Bank archive covering 145 years downstairs. Bankalar Cad. 11, Karaköy · Tue-Sat 11:00-19:00, Sun 11:00-18:00, closed Mondays · free admission

old_cards.name: Salt Research
old_cards.teaser: An open archive inside the bank that financed the city it later lost.
old_cards.body: Salt's research library occupies the Alexandre Vallaury building on Bankalar Caddesi that once housed the Imperial Ottoman Bank, and it holds that bank's own archive along with collections on art, architecture and design, and city, society and economy. Much is digitised and searchable from anywhere. Walk out and the Camondo Stairs are a minute away, built in the 1870s by the Ottoman-Venetian Jewish banker Abraham Salomon Camondo. Salt Galata, Bankalar Caddesi 11, Karaköy 34421 · Tue-Sat 11.00-19.00 · free · archives at saltresearch.org

old_cards.name: Çadır Köşkü, Yıldız Park
old_cards.teaser: A sultan's private garden, two pavilions, and a glass of çay.
old_cards.body: Abdülhamid II walled the outer garden of Yıldız Palace and filled it with artificial lakes, summer houses and a porcelain factory that is still going. Two of those pavilions, Çadır and Malta, now work as cafés inside what has since become a public park of some 368,000 square metres — breakfast, lunch, or a glass of tea under the trees, run by the municipal operator BELTUR along with the park's other restaurants. The climb from the Beşiktaş gate is steep enough that nobody arrives wanting to open a laptop. Yıldız Park, Beşiktaş · Çadır and Malta pavilions · public park
